title: Building a simple padded headboard from plywood and foam
subtitle: Cut a plywood panel, pad it with foam and wadding, and cover with an upholstery fabric for a wall-fixed headboard
excerpt: How to build a padded upholstered headboard from plywood, foam, dacron wadding, and furnishing fabric. Covers cutting the plywood shape, gluing the foam, stapling the fabric, and wall-fixing the finished headboard.
sourceNotes: Traditional upholstery construction practice. Period soft furnishings manuals (pre-1928 public domain).

glossaryTerms.definition: A polyester fibre wadding sold in rolls, used in upholstery to wrap over foam pads before covering with fabric. Dacron softens the outline of the foam, prevents the foam corners from showing through the cover fabric, and adds a small amount of extra cushioning. One layer of 50 g/m2 Dacron is the standard headboard application.

content.text: A padded headboard is a plywood panel covered with foam,

, and fabric stapled to the back. The plywood gives the shape; the foam provides the padding; the Dacron softens the foam edges. A finished headboard is wall-fixed through a batten fixed to the back of the board.

Cut a headboard panel from 18 mm structural plywood to the bed width plus 50 mm either side (for a standard UK king size, 1550 mm wide). The height is typically 700 to 900 mm above the mattress top. Mark any curved top edge with a compass or template and cut with the jigsaw. Sand all edges smooth with the sanding block.
Glue the foam to the plywood

Cut a foam sheet to the same shape as the plywood (or slightly larger, to be trimmed with the utility knife after gluing). Use a spray upholstery adhesive to bond the foam to the plywood face. Apply adhesive to both surfaces, allow 30 seconds to become tacky, then press the foam onto the plywood and hold firmly for one minute. For a generous finish, add a second layer of 25 mm foam on top of the first.

Cut a piece of Dacron wadding 150 mm larger than the headboard on all sides. Lay the headboard foam-down on the wadding. Pull the wadding up and over the back of the plywood and staple with 10 mm T50 staples at 50 mm intervals, starting at the top centre and working outward. Pull the wadding firm but not so tight that the foam compresses noticeably. At the corners, fold the wadding into a neat pleat and staple.

Repeat the stapling process with the cover fabric, cutting it 150 mm larger than the headboard on all sides. Work from the centre of each edge outward, pulling the fabric firmly and evenly so no wrinkles appear on the face. Staple every 40 to 50 mm. Fold the corners neatly (a hospital corner fold works well for a square corner; a series of small pleats works for a curved edge).

Fix a 100 x 25 mm timber batten horizontally to the wall at the correct height using the drill and masonry plugs. Fix a second batten to the back of the headboard. Hang the headboard batten over the wall batten; the two battens interlock to support the weight of the headboard against the wall.

attrs.symptom: Fabric wrinkles show on the face of the headboard
attrs.cause: Fabric not pulled evenly: one area was pulled tighter than the opposite side.
attrs.fix: Remove the staples on the wrinkled side and re-staple, pulling from the centre outward and checking the face frequently as you go.

attrs.symptom: Foam corners are visible through the fabric
attrs.cause: No Dacron layer used, or Dacron is too thin.
attrs.fix: Add a second layer of Dacron wadding over the corners before re-covering. The Dacron rounds the foam edges and removes the square-corner shadow.
